name: interpreter-as-data
intent: Represent every effect a program needs as an immutable data value - a closed set of operation descriptions plus pure constructors - so the program itself is a value that separate interpreters execute, letting the same program run against production effects, in-memory test doubles, logs or replays without changing a line of business logic.
problem: Business logic performs I/O, clock reads, randomness and network calls inline, so it can only run against the real world: tests must install mocks and still execute effects, a step cannot be replayed, audited, dry-run or simulated, and a second execution strategy (batch, retry, sandbox) means editing the logic. The recurring trigger is that a slice of logic must produce effects through a boundary that varies by environment - test vs. production being only the first pair - while the logic itself stays pure, inspectable and equal-comparable.
context: Applies where effects are the variable part of a program: application cores over repositories, gateways, clocks and loggers; runtimes that already interpret commands (Elm/Redux-style UI, saga middleware, workflow engines); query or rule front-ends whose trees are translated by providers rather than executed; and pipelines that must be logged, replayed, dry-run or sandboxed. It fits ecosystems where a closed set of operations can be expressed as a variant, union, record hierarchy or sealed interface with total matching, and it matters most when a second interpreter is actually coming - tests, previews, simulations, alternate backends.
benefits: Effects become inspectable values: a program can be logged, serialized, diffed, transformed, replayed and asserted on with plain equality before anything happens, so tests check the description instead of mocking collaborators.
Description and execution are separated: the business core depends only on the operation algebra, and the concrete clock, store, client or logger is chosen once at the boundary.
Interpreters are additive: production, in-memory, dry-run, logging, replaying, retrying or sandboxed execution are separate folds over the same program, each of them testable on its own.
New execution strategies do not touch business logic, and new programs reuse the existing interpreters.
Effects are explicit in types and in data: what a program may do is a closed, reviewable set, which is the natural basis for sandboxing, permission checks and effect budgets.
Programs compose as ordinary values (map/flatMap/sequence), so orchestration stays pure, and stack-safe execution is available where the runner trampolines.
tradeoffs: Three artifacts to maintain instead of one: the operation algebra, the constructors that build programs, and at least one interpreter - real overhead for logic with one effect and one runtime.
Interpreter drift: if the test interpreter's semantics diverge from production, the suite goes green while production breaks; the pattern buys testability, not correctness.

Interpreted execution costs allocation, indirection and dispatch per step and typically runs an order of magnitude slower than direct calls, and free-monad runners add heap-allocated trampolines to stay stack-safe.

Every new operation must be handled by every interpreter: growing the operation set is the expensive direction, and coproducts or effect stacks (Data types a la carte, FreeT/EitherT) are needed once algebras multiply.
Debugging crosses a boundary: stack traces point into folds and dispatch tables rather than into the business step that failed, which complicates debugging and profiling.

The vocabulary (free monad, natural transformation, foldMap, algebra vs. interpreter) is a barrier for teams without a functional background, and any program that is stored or shipped becomes a versioned contract.
The pattern does not remove the production implementation: the real effectful interpreter still has to be written, now behind an extra layer.

participants.responsibility: The closed set of value types (or the single variant/union type) naming every effect a program may describe - Get, Put, Log, Now - carrying only data and no behaviour: the interface between programs and interpreters.

A composed value of operations (free monad, generator of yielded descriptors, or plain collection) built by the client; it performs nothing on construction, can be stored, compared, replayed and re-interpreted.
Pure helper (liftF, a data-class constructor, a plain function) that lifts one operation into the program type so business code reads like direct calls while producing values instead of effects.

A total fold, natural transformation or switch mapping each operation to a concrete effect in a target runtime - production client, in-memory fake, logger, replayer; one interpreter per execution strategy.

The single place that pairs a program with a chosen interpreter and executes it (foldMap into a monad, middleware dispatch, framework runtime), owning the real side effects, retries, timeouts and error handling.

use_cases: Application cores that must be tested without I/O: repositories, payment gateways, clocks and loggers are operations, the test interpreter is an in-memory map plus a list, and the production interpreter wires the real clients.
UI and state runtimes in the Elm/Redux style: actions, commands and subscriptions are values the framework runtime interprets, which is why reducer tests are plain data assertions.

Saga and workflow orchestration: a generator or process manager yields step descriptions and a runtime performs them, enabling mock-free tests, retries, compensations and replay of long-running flows.

Query, rule and expression front-ends: trees built by user code are translated by providers (LINQ to SQL, JPA criteria, ORM query plans) rather than executed by the builder, so the same tree can target several backends.
Dry-run, simulation and audit modes for operational code: the same program is interpreted against a logging or capturing interpreter to preview changes or to satisfy audit requirements.
Sandboxed extension points: plugins or user scripts submit programs made of operations as data, which the host validates and interprets with restricted effects instead of running arbitrary code.
Effectful infrastructure jobs (ETL, provisioning) that need retry or rollback: because the program is data, the runner can re-interpret it after a failure or invert it for compensation.

Event-sourcing and CQRS backends: commands are programs (closed algebra of Append, Project, Emit), the event store is one interpreter, a projection rebuild is another, and a replay after schema migration is a third — all sharing identical command logic.

ML pipeline orchestration: training and inference pipelines describe data transforms, model calls, and metric writes as operations; a dry-run interpreter captures the data shape graph without executing GPUs, while a production interpreter runs the full pipeline.

Multi-cloud and provider-abstracted infrastructure: the algebra names generic operations (Compute, Store, Notify); cloud-specific interpreters implement them against AWS, GCP or Azure SDKs, letting the same program target any provider.

Plugin and scripting engines: untrusted scripts are programs built from a host-defined safe algebra; the host's interpreter validates each operation against a policy (allowed modules, rate limits, data boundaries) before execution, converting the data form into a security boundary.

Game development: game-logic commands (Move, Spawn, Score) are data; an authoritative server interpreter applies them, while a replay/debug interpreter records every step for deterministic replay, and a test interpreter validates game invariants without a running game loop.

Kubernetes controllers and custom resources: manifests and desired-state objects are declarative descriptions that reconciliation controllers repeatedly interpret against observed cluster state, so the same data-driven contract supports convergence, retries and alternate test controllers.

Terraform's plan/apply workflow: configuration and a saved execution plan are data that Terraform first analyzes and then interprets through provider APIs, allowing review, dry-run planning and exact later application without changing the configuration.

AWS Step Functions: Amazon States Language JSON state-machine definitions describe Task, Choice and Fail operations that the managed runtime interprets, separating workflow structure from service integrations and enabling validation before execution.
avoid_when: One effect and one implementation exist: injecting an interface (repository, client) is smaller and just as testable - reach for this pattern when a second interpretation is actually coming.
The effect sequence never needs to be inspected, stored or replayed: plain functions, callbacks, promises/async-await or coroutines describe the steps with far less ceremony.
The code sits in a performance-critical inner loop: per-step interpretation overhead dominates, so write direct code and keep the pattern at the orchestration boundary.

The operation set changes every sprint and interpreters multiply: each new operation then edits every interpreter, and a tagless-final encoding or a simple strategy interface absorbs that churn better.
The team cannot adopt the vocabulary or library (free monad, foldMap, natural transformation): a plain interface plus a test double stays maintainable where an unfamiliar abstraction does not.

Effects depend intimately on live host state (cursor windows, transaction handles) that cannot be modelled as values: keep such handles in the interpreter's state instead of forcing them into the algebra.
anti_patterns: "Free monad for everything": reifying effects where plain injection suffices, so every feature ships an algebra and an interpreter for one runtime and zero intended reuse.

Programs that perform effects while being constructed: calling the client inside a constructor or smart constructor (`call(api.fetch(x))` instead of `call(api.fetch, x)`) - the description is no longer a value and the test story collapses.
Interpreters that silently disagree: a fake interpreter with convenient-but-wrong semantics (no failures, no ordering, no idempotency), which converts a testability win into false confidence.
A god-algebra shared by every subsystem: each interpreter must then handle operations it does not care about, and the shared operation set becomes the new coupling.
Re-implementing monad machinery by hand (custom flatMap, ad-hoc trampolines) instead of using the ecosystem's library - or, inversely, importing a free-monad library for a two-operation algebra.

Interpreting untrusted programs with eval/exec or unrestricted effects instead of a validated, closed interpreter: the data form invites exactly this shortcut and re-opens injection and resource-exhaustion risks.
Ignoring stack safety: recursive interpreter folds without trampolining blow the stack on deep or generated programs.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: description (the program as data) and execution (the interpreter) are different responsibilities in different places.
Dependency inversion: business logic depends on the abstract operation algebra and the runner, never on concrete clients, clocks or loggers.
Functional core, imperative shell: pure program construction inside, effectful interpretation at the boundary.
Explicit effects over ambient state: every effect a program can perform is named in the algebra and handled by a total interpreter.
Open/closed, asymmetrically: new interpreters do not modify programs (open for extension), while new operations touch every interpreter - a deliberate, visible trade.
Make illegal states unrepresentable: a closed operation set plus exhaustive interpretation turns "unhandled effect" into a build error wherever the language can prove coverage.
best_practices: Keep operations as plain data — fields, identifiers and values only; when an operation must reference a function (Call(fn, args)), record the reference as data instead of invoking it.
Expose one pure smart constructor per operation and never let construction touch the real world.

Write interpreters as total folds: exhaustive matching, or an explicit throwing default where the language cannot prove coverage, so a new operation fails in the build or in one dedicated test rather than silently.
Always ship a first-class in-memory/test interpreter plus a logging one, and keep their semantics mirrored to production (share code where possible) to limit drift.

Choose the lightest encoding that satisfies the requirement: descriptor objects for orchestration, a free-monad/effect library only when composition across monads, retargeting or stack safety is genuinely needed, and tagless-final when no data is needed.
Test programs by asserting on their values and interpreters by asserting on their effects; validate and version any program that crosses a trust or storage boundary.
Trampoline or depth-bound the interpreter, and add step budgets/timeouts for programs that can be unbounded.

Validate interpreter semantics coverage with property-based testing: generate random programs, run both production and test interpreters, and assert equality of outcomes — catches interpreter drift before it reaches production.

Version the algebra alongside the program: a stored/replayed program pinned to an older algebra version may skip operations or run with wrong semantics when interpreted by a newer interpreter; treat the algebra as a schema.

Thread interpreter state carefully: an in-memory interpreter holding mutable collections is not thread-safe by default; prefer immutable data structures or explicit synchronization for concurrent program evaluation.
When composing algebras via coproducts (EitherK / FreeT), keep interpreters per-algebra and combine them with natural transformation composition rather than merging logic into one god-interpreter.

For programs that cross a network or persistence boundary, serialize the program (JSON, protobuf) and validate the algebra version before interpreting — an attacker who can craft programs can trigger interpreter bugs if input validation is absent.

Profile the interpreter's allocation pattern: free-monad programs over deep operations allocate heavily on the heap; consider a compiled interpreter (a flat switch over operation tags that carries a mutable state bundle) for hot paths.

pitfalls: Executing while constructing: a constructor that performs the effect destroys the data property the whole pattern rests on.
Handling a missing operation case with a silent default (no-op or zero) instead of a failure, so new operations run with wrong semantics.
Not writing a test interpreter that mirrors production semantics — interpreter drift is the pattern's characteristic failure mode.
Interpreting deeply nested or generated programs recursively without trampolining or a depth bound.

Space leaks from lazy interpretation: free-monad folds over suspended structures (FreeT wrapping IO) retain thunks; force strictness where the program is consumed, or use a compiled interpreter that processes operations strictly.

Silent serialization breakage: programs serialized as JSON with function references (Call('httpGet', ...)) become invalid if the function signature changes; prefer self-contained operation data or pinned schema versions.

Effect attribution in async interpreters: when an interpreter spawns concurrent tasks, errors may appear in the wrong operation's context; thread operation IDs through the async stack and include them in error reports.

Thread-safety of interpreter state: an in-memory interpreter with mutable accumulators (list of effects, call count) is unsafe under concurrent foldMap; use immutable state passthrough (State/Writer monad transformers) or lock-free concurrent structures.

Wrong move: use a free-monad representation for a short, single-runtime call chain -> allocation, bind traversal and interpreter indirection can dominate without providing retargeting or replay -> instead inject the dependency directly or compile the description into a flat loop when no second interpreter is required.

Wrong move: model reconciliation as a one-shot imperative script and assume each described effect runs exactly once -> a controller-style interpreter may retry or reorder work, duplicating non-idempotent side effects -> instead make operations idempotent and encode convergence, retry and deduplication semantics at the effect boundary.
